speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Kawasaki disease is also the most common cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If left untreated, about 15%-20% of cases develop coronary aneurysms and ectasia, and the risk of ischemic heart disease and sudden death.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The background facts to the case are as follows.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: On 25 February 2013, the patient, a one-year-old child, was hospitalised at Gleneagles hospital with high fever for three days and red eyes, besides other symptoms.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The paediatrician who was on call at the hospital, Dr Chia Foong Lin, attended to the child and diagnosed the case as a viral infection.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Two days later, on 27 February, or the fifth day of the child's fever, the child was noted to be fretful, had red lips and developed a rash.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: On 28 February, the following day, he had a spike of fever in the morning and red and cracked lips.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia considered the possibility of Kawasaki disease and looked for the full features of Kawasaki disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, she did not conduct any supportive tests for Kawasaki disease and did not share this with the parents.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia's diagnosis remained as viral infection as there were no full features of Kawasaki disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: On 1 March, the fifth day in the hospital and the seventh day of the child's fever, the child was discharged by Dr Chia as the fever appeared to have settled.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: According to Dr Chia, the red eyes improved and no rashes were seen but his lips were still slightly red and cracked.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The diagnosis by Dr Chia was again viral infection.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: On 3 March, which was the ninth day of the child's fever, the child was reviewed by Dr Chia as an outpatient at her clinic.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia was informed by the parents that the fever had continued in the two days after discharge although, according to Dr Chia, the red eyes and the rashes had resolved and the child's lips had improved.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The history of the progression of the child's symptoms and signs, including prolonged fever, red eye, rash and red lips were suggestive of Kawasaki disease which should have prompted Dr Chia to carry out supportive tests, but Dr Chia still maintained that it was viral fever and did not order any supportive tests.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The next day, on 4 March, the child's parents decided to seek a second opinion and went to consult another paediatrician as the child continued to have high fever.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: On examination, she noted that the child was irritable and had a rash on the upper body.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The second paediatrician also noted redness in the child's palms and soles, prominent lymph nodes on the right neck and discovered a heart murmur.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: All these were signs suggestive of Kawasaki disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: She ordered the blood tests which supported the diagnosis of Kawasaki disease and an echocardiogram which showed that the blood vessels of the heart was already affected.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Fortunately, the child responded well from the treatment for Kawasaki disease and the fever settled.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The child's mother then filed a complaint with the Singapore Medical Council (SMC).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In accordance with the Medical Registration Act, the SMC convened a Complaints Committee.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: After conducting its own investigations, the Complaints Committee concluded that a formal inquiry by a Disciplinary Tribunal (DT) was necessary.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: A DT was convened comprising two senior doctors and a lawyer.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: During its inquiry, the DT also considered the opinions of two expert witnesses.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The DT noted that there were already well accepted international guidelines for the diagnosis of Kawasaki disease since 2004.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Based on these international guidelines, the child presented with signs and symptoms which should be investigated further for Kawasaki disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In deciding on the sentence, the DT considered eight precedents relating to doctors who had missed or given a wrong diagnosis, failed to provide adequate advice and/or failed to provide adequate and timely treatment to patients.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The DT noted that six of the precedents were dealt with by a suspension instead of a fine.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The DT also took into account the seniority of Dr Chia and that she was an experienced paediatrician of 23 years' standing.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia appealed to the High Court against the DT's decision.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The High Court noted that Dr Chia had not pleaded guilty to the charge and that the disease faced was not uncommon.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Taking these factors, as well as the precedents into consideration, the High Court found the order of three months' suspension to be appropriate.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The appeal was then dismissed by the High Court.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Lim asked if MOH advocates doctors to send all cases for detailed diagnostic tests to avoid misdiagnosing rare medical conditions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Such defensive medicine practice deviates from good clinical practice.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Lim also asked if the Ministry should issue standard practice guidelines on diagnosis for all potentially rare illnesses.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is neither possible nor practical for MOH to issue guidelines for all rare diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As part of their work, doctors are expected to exercise good clinical judgement to manage patients appropriately.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Clinical judgement is dependent on the seniority of the doctor, the area of practice and experience, clinical presentation of each patient and the facts and circumstances surrounding each case.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For cases which are complex or for which the treating doctors are unsure, they can also discuss with other colleagues on the most appropriate management of the case.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is important for doctors to keep abreast of medical knowledge and international guidelines based on the recommendations of medical experts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Hence, SMC requires all doctors in the public and private sectors to have mandatory continuing medical education.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our hospitals and institutions also have teaching, training and peer review to enable doctors to maintain and upgrade their skills.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is the exact blood test he is referring to?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Because, as far as I know, there is no specific blood test for Kawasaki disease in the first place.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last of all is that it is very common.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I mean, for all parents here who have children, to find a child with fever, with a rash.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Does it mean that every single child with rash and fever has to be sent for a cardiac scan in future?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I think that is the fear that we have now.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is the impact of this verdict on current healthcare costs?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Frequently, we hear complaints from our residents, from our patients that the investigation costs are going up − tests are very expensive.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, every single blood test, every single scan, every single MRI you do, is expensive.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Every single headache could be a brain tumour.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are we going to investigate every single headache with a scan as well?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I think these are the pertinent questions that we are asking.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is MOH monitoring whether there are signs of defensive medicine being practiced in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Currently, if you look at the outpatient bill, what proportion of the outpatient bill is investigation cost versus consultation and medication cost?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is the investigation cost portion increasing over the years?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: These are the things that I think MOH should be looking at as well.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Though non-specific for Kawasaki disease, it is a supportive investigation that helps in the diagnosis of Kawasaki disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And, of course, in cases where Kawasaki disease is highly suspected, there is also a need to order echo-cardiogram to assess the coronary vessels to look for any aneurysms or dilatation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The American Heart Association has come up with international guidelines in the management of Kawasaki disease as well as the evaluation of incomplete Kawasaki disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If you look at the literature, incomplete Kawasaki disease is more common in children who are of a very young age, which was what this child had	in this case − incomplete Kawasaki disease.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: So, in this case, the patient does have persistent fever, the patient has skin rash, bilateral sore eyes as well as cracked lips.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: So, this patient actually had more than two signs; he had three signs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Based on the international guidelines, supportive tests, such as C-reactive protein and echo-cardiogram, should have been ordered.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As to the Member's second comment on whether every child with fever or rash should therefore be investigated for Kawasaki disease, the answer is obviously no.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But it is important for doctors to have the enhanced awareness that should the patient develop other symptoms or signs that point towards Kawasaki disease, further investigation would be warranted.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I also understand that there are many doctors who are concerned with the verdict and judgement of this case.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My advice to doctors is that they should stay calm and not overreact.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Because, very often, when doctors read the headlines, they will jump to the conclusion that, "Oh, if I miss a fever and therefore miss a Kawasaki disease diagnosis, I will be suspended for three months".

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: One of the common questions that Dr Lim had alluded to is: "Should I investigate every child who presents with fever or a rash for Kawasaki disease?" Of course, like I mentioned previously, the answer is no.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: That would actually be tantamount to very poor clinical judgement and defensive medicine.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The advice to doctors is that we should fall back on basics first.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Getting a good history and a thorough and proper clinical examination is critical in the practice of medicine.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Consider any international guidelines available in the evaluation and management of the condition at hand.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the case of Kawasaki disease, the international guidelines on the evaluation of suspected incomplete Kawasaki disease and the diagnosis of management of Kawasaki disease from the American Heart Association is internationally well-known and accepted and has been there since 2004.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If the doctor is unsure or if the case is complex, please do not hesitate to discuss with other more experienced colleagues on the most appropriate management of the case.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH is monitoring this very carefully and, like I mentioned, if doctors were to practise good clinical judgement, we do not have to go towards defensive medicine.
